pl-l4d33c1-d1e115.summary: Asks whether the ancient fathers, who are read to have had several wives or concubines at once, sinned.

pl-l4d33c1-d1e118.summary: Answers that the Creator's dispensation varies with the times. From the beginning marriage was between two, Adam and Eve, and would have remained so had the first parents obeyed; their sons and daughters married one to one, siblings joining since there were no others. Lamech first had two wives, and is blamed for doing it from lust. Later, when nearly all served false gods and few worshipped God, it was provided that some take several wives lest worship and knowledge of God fail; so Abraham went in to the handmaid while his wife lived, Jacob joined free women and handmaids, and Lot's daughters used their drunken father.
claims: God's dispensation of marriage varies with the times.
Polygamy was allowed so that God's few worshippers would multiply.
Lamech's bigamy was blameworthy, being from lust.

pl-l4d33c1-d1e130.summary: Explains that when God chose Abraham and his sons as his people, leaving others in idolatry, multiplication of God's people was rightly sought through many women's fertility, since religion succeeded with blood; so the sterile woman was cursed in the Law, and priests were given marriage, office succeeding with family. Abraham and Jacob did not sin in seeking children from handmaids, but no one may now seek fertility beyond the conjugal debt by their example, since their marriages equal our virginity, while immoderate use of our marriages almost imitates the fornication of that time.
claims: Religion's succession by blood justified seeking many offspring.
The patriarchs' marriages equal our virginity in merit.

pl-l4d33c1-d1e143.summary: Quotes Augustine: it was not sin for the ancient just to use several women, nor against nature, since for begetting, not lust; nor against custom, since it was done then; nor against precept, since no law forbade it.
claims: Patriarchal polygamy violated neither nature, custom, nor precept.

pl-l4d33c1-d1e152.summary: Adds Augustine: Jacob's four wives are objected to, but when it was custom it was not crime; the patriarchs united for propagating succession, not lust, as the apostles delighted in hearers' admiration not from greed for praise but charity for spreading truth.
claims: The patriarchs sought succession, not pleasure.

pl-l4d33c1-d1e161.summary: Adds Augustine: in ancient times, when our salvation's mystery was veiled, the just married from the duty of propagation, led by piety, not overcome by lust, and could have abstained if they wished; one man could have several wives, whom he held more chastely than any of ours holds one.
claims: The patriarchs held several wives more chastely than men now hold one.

pl-l4d33c1-d1e170.summary: Quotes Ambrose on Sarah's giving Hagar to Abraham: Abraham lived before the Law of Moses and the Gospel, so did not sin against the Law not yet given; he preferred the handmaid's bed not from wandering lust or beauty but from desire for posterity, when after the flood the human race and religion were scarce; Lot's daughters too sought posterity lest the race fail, the public good cloaking private fault.
claims: Abraham sinned against no law and acted for posterity.

pl-l4d33c1-d1e194.summary: Quotes Augustine: as the just man, though desiring to be with Christ, takes food out of duty to others, so union with women by right of marriage was dutiful for holy men, not lustful; what food is for a man's health, intercourse is for the race's, both with carnal delight, which, moderated by temperance and directed to natural use, cannot be lust; as unlawful food sustains life sinfully, so fornication seeks offspring sinfully, and as excessive appetite for lawful food, so venial intercourse in marriage.
claims: Intercourse is to the race what food is to the individual.
Moderated delight in natural use is not lust.

pl-l4d33c1.summary: Asks whether the ancient fathers who had several wives or concubines sinned. God's dispensation varies with the times: marriage began between two, and would have remained so had the first parents obeyed; Adam's children married siblings, one to one; Lamech first took two wives, blamed for lust; later, when nearly all served false gods, God permitted several wives so the few worshippers would multiply, hence Abraham, Jacob, and Lot's daughters. Since the succession of religion followed blood, fertility was sought, and priests married. They did not sin, though we may not follow them; their marriages equal our virginity. Augustine and Ambrose: it was not against nature, custom, or precept, being for begetting, not lust; Abraham acted before the Law, from desire for posterity, not lust; as food sustains a man, intercourse sustains the race, and moderated delight is not lust.
claims: The patriarchs' polygamy was not sinful, being dispensed for multiplying God's people.
God's dispensation of marriage varies with the times.
Their unions sought offspring, not lust.
Their example may not be followed now.
